questions.question: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Why is it still 'accelerated motion'?
questions.solution: Acceleration is the rate of change of VELOCITY, and velocity is a vector: constant speed but continuously changing direction means the velocity changes — hence acceleration. The acceleration (v²/r) points to the centre, perpendicular to velocity, changing direction but never magnitude.

questions.question: In a turning bus you feel thrown outward. Is there an outward force acting on you? Explain both frames.
questions.solution: In the ground frame: no outward force — your body tends to go straight (inertia) while the bus turns inward under you. In the bus's rotating frame, we INVENT a centrifugal force (mv²/r outward) to make Newton's laws work — a fictitious force from the accelerating frame. The sensation is real; the outward force is not.

questions.question: A bucket of water is whirled in a vertical circle. Where is the string tension maximum and minimum, and why doesn't the water fall at the top?
questions.solution: Bottom: T − mg = mv²/r → T = mv²/r + mg (maximum). Top: T + mg = mv²/r → T = mv²/r − mg (minimum). At the top the water doesn't fall because gravity itself provides (part of) the centripetal force — as long as v ≥ √(gr), the required acceleration exceeds g and the water presses on the bucket bottom.

questions.concept: Centripetal force is not a new force
questions.question: When a car turns, what physical force plays the role of the centripetal force? Why can't 'centripetal force' appear in a free-body diagram as its own arrow?
questions.solution: Friction between tyres and road supplies the inward force mv²/r. 'Centripetal' names a ROLE (net inward force), not a new interaction — listing it separately double-counts. A free-body diagram shows only real forces (weight, normal, friction); their resultant happens to point to the centre.

questions.concept: Angle of banking and speed limit
questions.question: Why does the safe speed on an unbanked curve drop when the road is wet, in terms of the v²/r relation?
questions.solution: Required centripetal force mv²/r must be supplied by friction, whose maximum is μmg — giving v_max = √(μgr). Wet road lowers μ, so v_max falls as √μ. Doubling speed quadruples the required force (v²), which is why speeding on curves is disproportionately dangerous.
